html:
The religion of the pharaoh Akhenaten, who from about 1353 BCE made the Aten, the disc of the sun, the one god of Egypt. It was among the earliest experiments in worshipping a single god, and it was abandoned soon after his death.

Akhenaten, first called Amenhotep IV, cut off funds to the old temples. Agents hacked the name of Amun, the great god of Thebes, off monuments. He built a new capital at Amarna with open-air temples where the sun's rays could fall on the altars. Only the king and his queen Nefertiti could approach the Aten; everyone else worshipped through them. Art of the period became looser and more natural.

The Great Hymn to the Aten praises the sun as maker of all life, in lines that some compare to Psalm 104 in the Bible. Scholars still argue whether Atenism was true monotheism. After Akhenaten died, the boy king Tutankhaten renamed himself Tutankhamun and brought back Amun. Amarna was left empty, and later kings struck Akhenaten from the lists of the New Kingdom pharaohs.
